questions.prompt: A crossword clue of this module is printed as a pair: "not instrumental but …". Which word fills the squares?
questions.explanation: The module sorts family roles into two classes, instrumental and affective, and the clue asks for the second half of that pair, in the same class of word as the first: "affective". "affection" names the feeling itself and is a noun, while the words not instrumental but can only be followed by an adjective. "affectionate" is an adjective, but it describes a person who shows love, not a kind of role. "effective" is a different word altogether and means producing the result you were aiming at.

questions.prompt: A table has the three headings Verb, Noun and Adjective. One of its rows reads: (Verb) ___ · (Noun) satisfaction · (Adjective) satisfactory. Which word belongs in the empty cell?
questions.explanation: The empty cell stands in the Verb column, and the verb the whole family is built on is "satisfy": both satisfaction and satisfactory come from it. "satisfaction" is already printed in the Noun column, so writing it again would leave the Verb column empty. "satisfied" and "satisfying" are adjectives, and the Adjective column is filled: satisfied describes the person who feels it, satisfying describes what causes the feeling.

questions.prompt: A pupil has copied a sentence from the board without a single mark: "her father a canadian engineer spent every august in djerba". Which version restores it correctly?

options.text: Her father a Canadian engineer spent every August in Djerba.
Her father, a canadian engineer, spent every august in Djerba.
Her Father, a Canadian Engineer, spent every August in Djerba.
Her father, a Canadian engineer, spent every August in Djerba.

questions.explanation: A phrase slipped between the subject and its verb is closed by a comma on each side, a proper noun takes a capital, an adjective built on a proper noun keeps it, and so does the name of a month: "Her father, a Canadian engineer, spent every August in Djerba." The version without any comma lets the description run into the sentence, so the reader reaches spent before knowing where the subject ended. The version with a small c on canadian and a small a on august takes the capital off an adjective of nationality and off a month, and English keeps both. The version with Father and Engineer in capitals treats two ordinary common nouns as names, which no amount of respect for the man justifies.

questions.prompt: Complete this line with the phrasal verb that carries the meaning printed in brackets: "Hurry up and ___ one project; the deadline is on Friday." (settle on one choice)
questions.explanation: "decide on" is the phrasal verb that means settling on one choice among several, which is exactly the meaning in brackets and exactly what a deadline forces. "dream of" means having a fantasy of doing something, so the line would say she is imagining a project instead of choosing one. "look for" means seeking somebody or something that is missing, and no project is lost here. "take over" means assuming control of something somebody else was running, which is a change of hands, not a decision between projects.

questions.prompt: A neighbour offers to drive Dorra to the airport. She wants to answer that nothing obliges him to do it, since the bus passes her door. Which answer says exactly that?

options.text: You mustn't drive me — the bus passes my door.
You needn't drive me — the bus passes my door.
You needn't driving me — the bus passes my door.
You needn't to drive me — the bus passes my door.

questions.explanation: needn't expresses the absence of necessity and takes the bare verb after it, which gives "You needn't drive me". "You mustn't drive me" forbids him to drive her: mustn't closes the door, while needn't only says that nothing obliges him to walk through it. "You needn't to drive me" slips in a to, and a modal is never followed by one. "You needn't driving me" puts an -ing form where the bare verb belongs, exactly as must and should refuse one.
